zuproto

Overview

Protocol Buffers is a binary format for structured data. gRPC APIs, Kafka topics, transit feeds, telemetry pipelines and machine-learning datasets all use it. Its bytes mean nothing without the schema that describes them, and reading them in R has meant installing the C++ protobuf library and handling each message as its own object.

zuproto reads and writes any protobuf message in R. It works from the compiled schema, and turns thousands of messages into one data frame.

  • Any message type, no generated code. Give zuproto a descriptor set, the schema as protoc --descriptor_set_out or buf build writes it, and it decodes and encodes every type in it.
  • Many messages are columns. A list of messages, a length-delimited stream, or a message’s repeated field becomes a data frame, filled column by column in C.
  • No system library. zuproto bundles upb, the small C runtime under protobuf’s Python, Ruby and PHP implementations. It needs no libprotobuf, Abseil or other R package to install or run. protoc or buf is needed only once, to compile your schema.
  • R types where they fit. Enums are factors, Timestamp is POSIXct, Duration is difftime, and 64-bit integers can stay exact.
  • Careful with untrusted bytes. Input size, nesting depth, memory and rows are all capped, strings are checked as UTF-8, and an interrupted decode frees its memory.

Installation

zuproto is not on CRAN yet. Once it is, install it with:

install.packages("zuproto")

Until then, install the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zuproto")

Usage 

library(zuproto)

A pool holds the message types zuproto knows. Every pool starts with protobuf’s well-known types:

pool <- proto_pool()
pool
#> <proto_pool: 11 files, 61 message types>

R values become messages and back. A Timestamp is a POSIXct, and a Struct is a named list:

when <- as.POSIXct("2026-10-27 15:36:18", tz = "UTC")
bytes <- proto_encode(when, "google.protobuf.Timestamp", pool)
bytes
#> [1] 08 f2 89 83 d7 06
proto_decode(bytes, "google.protobuf.Timestamp", pool)
#> [1] "2026-10-27 15:36:18 UTC"

bytes <- proto_encode(
  list(station = "Bern", platform = 7, delayed = TRUE),
  "google.protobuf.Struct",
  pool
)
str(proto_decode(bytes, "google.protobuf.Struct", pool))
#> List of 3
#>  $ delayed : logi TRUE
#>  $ platform: num 7
#>  $ station : chr "Bern"

Protobuf’s JSON mapping goes both ways. A Timestamp is an RFC 3339 string in JSON:

json <- proto_to_json(
  proto_encode(when, "google.protobuf.Timestamp", pool),
  "google.protobuf.Timestamp",
  pool
)
json
#> [1] "\"2026-10-27T15:36:18Z\""
proto_decode(
  proto_from_json(json, "google.protobuf.Timestamp", pool),
  "google.protobuf.Timestamp",
  pool
)
#> [1] "2026-10-27 15:36:18 UTC"

Many messages become a data frame. A descriptor set is itself a protobuf message, a FileDescriptorSet, so the one zuproto ships for the well-known types can be read as a table. Each row is a .proto file, with the number of message types it defines at the top level:

wkt <- system.file("descriptors", "wkt.binpb", package = "zuproto")
files <- proto_decode_df(
  wkt,
  "google.protobuf.FileDescriptorSet",
  pool,
  field = "file"
)
data.frame(
  name = files$name,
  messages = vapply(files$message_type, NROW, integer(1))
)
#>                                    name messages
#> 1             google/protobuf/any.proto        1
#> 2  google/protobuf/source_context.proto        1
#> 3            google/protobuf/type.proto        5
#> 4             google/protobuf/api.proto        3
#> 5      google/protobuf/descriptor.proto       23
#> 6        google/protobuf/duration.proto        1
#> 7           google/protobuf/empty.proto        1
#> 8      google/protobuf/field_mask.proto        1
#> 9          google/protobuf/struct.proto        3
#> 10      google/protobuf/timestamp.proto        1
#> 11       google/protobuf/wrappers.proto        9

Your own schema goes in the same way. Compile it once with protoc or buf, then load the descriptor set. Here it is with the live trip updates for Switzerland’s public transport, in the GTFS Realtime format. The code is not run here; the output is from 27 October 2026:

pool <- proto_pool("gtfs-realtime.binpb")
trips <- proto_decode_df(
  "trip-updates.binpb",
  "transit_realtime.FeedMessage",
  pool,
  field = "entity"
)
table(trips$trip_update$trip$schedule_relationship)[1:4]
#>
#>   SCHEDULED       ADDED UNSCHEDULED    CANCELED
#>       15187         245           0         144

Every function that converts a message takes the value, the message type’s full name and the pool, in that order.

Learn more

  • Live Swiss trains with GTFS Realtime works through a real feed: compiling the schema, fetching the data, and turning trips and stop delays into tables.
  • Three articles open machine-learning files without the library that wrote them: an ONNX model, its layers and trained weights; TensorFlow files, a SavedModel, TFRecord training data and TensorBoard logs; and a Core ML model, a decision tree read as a table.
  • The reference index lists every function. ?proto_decode maps protobuf types to R types, ?proto_decode_df says how fields become columns, and ?zuproto-conditions lists the errors and warnings.

Related work

zuproto bundles upb and utf8_range from protobuf v36.2. Its CI runs protobuf’s conformance test suite, with the tests zuproto is expected to fail listed and explained, and the test fixtures come from Python’s protobuf. RProtoBuf binds the C++ protobuf library and handles each message as an object. protolite serialises a fixed set of schemas: R objects, GeoJSON and Mapbox vector tiles.
